What causes volcanoes to erupt? – Avery, age 8, Los Angeles On Nov. 27, 2022, Mauna Loa – the world’s largest active volcano – erupted on the island of Hawaii. For days, fountains of lava, boiling at more than 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,100 degrees Celsius), spewed upward and flowed down the mountain’s sides. For tens of millions of people around the world, the videos were a mesmerizing sight. Then, a few weeks later, the eruption ended. Fortunately, there were no known deaths, and no major property damage. About a week later, Mount Semeru in East Java, Indonesia, erupted a mix of ash, gas and hot rocks. The plumes rose a mile above the mountain’s summit. Thousands living in the vicinity were evacuated; many wore masks to protect themselves from the ash-filled air. Mount Semeru has continued to erupt for months. I am a geologist who studies minerals in volcanic rocks. I want to learn more about what causes volcanoes to erupt. passages.text: the surface, Earth is always moving and changing. Generally, scientists don't try to stop volcanoes from erupting. They are a natural part of the Earth. But monitoring volcanoes is critical. People need an early warning of an eruption so they can move out of harm's way. While we cannot predict the exact time of an eruption, scientists are learning more about what causes them, and how to protect people who live near them. What's critical: warning systems for lahars, planned evacuation routes in areas threatened by volcanoes, and excellent communication between the scientists at volcanic monitoring stations and government agencies who can let people know when a volcano is about to go. passages.text: Volcanic eruptions are caused by the movement of molten rock, or magma, beneath the Earth's crust. This process is driven primarily by the heat from the Earth's core, which melts rock in the mantle, creating magma. This magma is less dense than the surrounding solid rock, causing it to rise through cracks and fractures in the Earth's crust. What Causes Volcano to Erupt? Several factors contribute to volcanic eruptions: Plate Tectonics The Earth's lithosphere is divided into tectonic plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere beneath. When these plates move, they can interact in ways that lead to volcanic activity. For example, at divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, allowing magma to rise and fill the gap. At convergent boundaries, one plate subducts beneath another, melting and generating magma that can lead to eruptions. Pressure Build-up As magma rises, gases dissolved in it come out of solution and expand, increasing pressure within the magma chamber. When the pressure becomes too great, it can fracture the overlying rock, allowing magma to escape to the surface explosively. The balance between gas production, gas escape, and the strength of the surrounding rock helps determine whether an eruption occurs and how explosive it becomes. Pressure does not simply build without limit until every volcano bursts. Volcanic systems are dynamic. Magma can migrate, gas can escape, fractures can open, and underground reservoirs can change shape. These processes can relieve pressure before an eruption begins. Why volcanic gases can make eruptions explosive Magma contains dissolved volatile substances, especially water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur-bearing gases. Their amounts vary with the magma’s source, composition, and history. Water vapor is often particularly important in explosive eruptions. Deep underground, high pressure allows substantial quantities of water to remain dissolved in magma. As the magma rises, falling pressure causes the water to form bubbles. Those bubbles expand as the magma approaches the surface. If the magma is able to release gas easily, it may erupt relatively gently. How tectonic plates influence volcanic eruptions The movement of Earth’s tectonic plates helps determine where magma forms and what kinds of volcanoes develop. At divergent boundaries, plates move apart, allowing hot mantle rock to rise and undergo decompression melting. This process supplies magma to mid-ocean ridges and some continental rift zones. Eruptions in these environments commonly produce basaltic lava, although volcanic behavior varies by location. At convergent boundaries, one plate may descend beneath another in a process called subduction. Water and other substances released from the sinking plate help generate magma in the mantle above it. As this magma rises through the crust, it can change composition, interact with surrounding rock, and accumulate dissolved gases. These conditions contribute to the explosive behavior associated with many volcanoes around the Pacific Ocean’s Ring of Fire. Some volcanoes form far from plate boundaries. At hotspots, rising mantle material supplies heat and magma to the overlying crust. Why volcanoes eventually stop erupting A volcanic eruption can slow or stop when the supply of magma decreases, pressure falls, pathways become blocked, or the remaining magma cools and solidifies. Gas may escape sufficiently to reduce the force driving the eruption, while fractures can close or become obstructed by cooled lava and other deposits. Some volcanoes erupt repeatedly because their magma supply is replenished. Others remain quiet for centuries or longer before becoming active again. A long period without eruptions does not necessarily mean that a volcano is extinct. Scientists distinguish between active, dormant, and extinct volcanoes, but these terms do not always have universally agreed definitions. An active volcano may be erupting or showing signs of ongoing volcanic activity. A dormant volcano has been quiet but may erupt again. An extinct volcano is generally considered unlikely to erupt again because its magma supply has effectively ended, although establishing that status with certainty can be difficult. passages.text: Volcanoes erupt when molten rock, gas, and other materials beneath Earth’s surface rise and escape through openings in the crust. The process is driven primarily by the movement of magma, the pressure exerted by dissolved gases, and the physical properties of the molten rock. Some eruptions unfold gradually, releasing streams of lava, while others produce explosive blasts of ash, rock fragments, and hot gas. The key to understanding volcanic eruptions is that magma does not simply rise because it is hot. Its movement depends on differences in density, the structure of the surrounding rock, the amount of gas it contains, and the conditions underground. When magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Whether it emerges gently or violently depends largely on how easily gases can escape as the magma rises. What happens beneath a volcano before an eruption? Most volcanic activity begins deep underground, where rock melts to form magma. This molten material accumulates in the Earth’s crust or rises from deeper regions of the mantle, the thick layer of hot rock beneath the crust. Why some volcanoes erupt explosively while others produce flowing lava The most important factors controlling eruption style include magma viscosity, gas content, the rate at which magma rises, and whether gases can escape before pressure becomes extreme. Viscosity describes a fluid’s resistance to flowing. Magma rich in silica generally has a more connected network of chemical structures, making it more viscous than many low-silica magmas. Highly viscous magma resists flow and can make it difficult for gas bubbles to rise and escape. Basaltic magma, which typically contains relatively little silica, is often less viscous and can flow readily. At many basaltic volcanoes, gases escape relatively efficiently, allowing lava to pour or spatter from vents and travel across the surrounding landscape. Such eruptions can still be dangerous, particularly when lava advances toward communities or infrastructure. Rhyolitic magma, which is rich in silica, is generally much more viscous. Carbon dioxide, for example, can begin separating from magma at greater depths than water under many conditions. Its release may influence how magma moves and how pressure changes within a volcanic system. Volcanic gases can also pose hazards without an explosive eruption. Carbon dioxide can accumulate in low-lying areas because it is denser than air, while sulfur dioxide can irritate the respiratory system and contribute to air pollution. Volcanic activity also releases gases and transfers heat from Earth’s interior to its surface. At the same time, eruptions can threaten lives, homes, transportation networks, crops, and water supplies. Lava flows can bury buildings and block roads. Ash can reduce visibility, contaminate water, damage machinery, and disrupt air travel. Pyroclastic density currents can destroy communities near a volcano, while lahars—rapid flows of water mixed with volcanic ash, rock, and other debris—can travel down valleys long after an eruption begins or even after it ends. The hazards vary with eruption style, the amount and type of material released, local topography, weather, and the distance between the volcano and populated areas. An eruption does not need to be exceptionally large to cause serious disruption, especially when ash or other hazards affect densely populated regions. Understanding what drives an eruption helps communities prepare for these risks. Monitoring systems, hazard maps, evacuation plans, and public communication can reduce exposure, although they cannot eliminate volcanic danger. passages.text: Rhyolitic magma, which is rich in silica, is generally much more viscous. It can trap gas and encourage pressure to build, making explosive eruptions more likely under suitable conditions. Some eruptions involving this type of magma produce towering columns of ash, while others generate thick lava domes. Andesitic magma falls between basaltic and rhyolitic magma in silica content, although actual behavior depends on temperature, crystals, gas content, and other factors. Volcanoes that produce andesitic magma can generate both lava flows and highly explosive eruptions. These categories describe general tendencies, not absolute rules. Basaltic magma can erupt explosively when gas release is rapid or when magma interacts with water. Silica-rich magma can sometimes erupt effusively, meaning that it produces lava flows rather than a major explosion, if its gas content and other conditions allow it. The presence of water outside the volcano can also change the outcome. When magma or hot volcanic material encounters groundwater, a lake, or seawater, the water may heat rapidly and turn to steam. This interaction can cause a steam-driven or magma-water explosion, depending on whether fresh magma is directly involved. Tectonic setting influences the supply and composition of magma, but it does not determine the precise timing or strength of an individual eruption. Those depend on conditions within the volcanic system, including magma movement, gas behavior, and the structure of the surrounding rock. What happens during a volcanic eruption An eruption begins when magma and volcanic gases find a pathway to the surface. The sequence can vary considerably, but many eruptions involve several connected processes. As magma rises, dissolved gases form bubbles and expand. The magma may push through existing fractures or create new ones, sometimes generating earthquakes and changing the shape of the ground. Once the magma reaches a vent, gas expansion and the force of rising material drive its release. In an effusive eruption, relatively fluid magma emerges and flows as lava. A volcano may initially produce lava, then become more explosive as gas accumulates or the magma’s properties change. Alternatively, an explosive phase may give way to less violent lava emission as pressure falls and gas escapes. Why volcanoes can erupt without much warning Volcanic systems can show signs of unrest before an eruption, but the warning period varies. Some volcanoes produce detectable changes over days or weeks, while others undergo longer periods of activity. In some cases, an eruption begins with little clearly detectable warning. Scientists monitor volcanoes for changes in earthquake activity, ground deformation, gas emissions, temperature, and surface activity. Each measurement reveals a different part of the system. Earthquakes can indicate rock fracturing or fluid movement, while deformation may reveal changes in underground pressure or magma volume. Changes in gas composition and emission rates can provide additional clues about magma movement. The challenge is that volcanic systems are complex, and similar signals can have different explanations. An increase in earthquakes may indicate magma rising, but it can also reflect the movement of hydrothermal fluids
